title: The four rounds
hook: he writes the four lavan, the wedding hymns that Sikh couples still walk around the Granth to (Suhi, ang 773)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Amritsar, the pool of nectar. Your line was a town around a pool. What sits in the middle of your days? Day fifty-six, the end of a week.

If you've ever been to a Sikh wedding, you've seen it. Morning, in the gurdwara. The couple sits before the Guru Granth Sahib, the scripture, resting on its raised seat. The bride holds one end of a long scarf, the groom the other. Then the musicians begin to sing, and the couple stands and walks slowly around the scripture, clockwise, the groom a step ahead, the scarf between them. They sit. The singing starts again. They walk again. Four times in all. Every one of those rounds is a hymn, and all four were written by the orphan from Lahore, Guru Ram Das. Today, the four rounds.
screen: `A MORNING WEDDING IN THE GURDWARA.` → `A SCARF BETWEEN THEM.` → `FOUR WALKS AROUND THE SCRIPTURE.`

segments.voice: They're called the lavan, the rounds. The hymn is in the scripture, in raga Suhi, and it has four stanzas. Each stanza is one round, and each describes a stage, in paraphrase. The first round is about the duties of a good life: following the Guru's teaching, living honestly, remembering God's name. The second is about meeting the true Guru; fear falls away, and the mind is humbled. In the third, the heart fills with longing and love, detached from the world's pull. In the fourth, the mind is at peace, and the soul and God are united as one. Here's the surprise: the lavan are about two marriages at once. On the surface, a husband and wife, walking into a shared life. Underneath, the soul's marriage to God, which is what Guru Ram Das is really singing about. So the couple isn't only promising themselves to each other. Together, they're walking the soul's path, round by round, with the scripture at the center. The Sikh wedding is called the Anand Karaj, the ceremony of bliss. Remember Anand? And it's usually closed with the Anand Sahib. And look back over the week. The baoli, water for all. First the row, even for an emperor. The manji, and she is not lesser. Anand, the song of bliss. Jetha, the orphan. Amritsar, the pool. And now four rounds, one life. Two Gurus, and one idea running through them: everyone at the same level, walking the same path, with the Word in the middle.
screen: `LAVAN — FOUR ROUNDS, FOUR STANZAS.` · `DUTY, THE GURU, LOVE, UNION.` · `TWO MARRIAGES AT ONCE.` · `THE ANAND KARAJ, CEREMONY OF BLISS.` · then, large: `FOUR ROUNDS, ONE LIFE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: think of a promise you keep. Settle, and breathe. Not one you've broken; one you keep. To a partner, a child, a friend, a parent, yourself. Maybe you've never said it out loud. Think about when you made it, and every time since that you've kept it, round after round. If you pray, you can give thanks for it. If not, just let yourself feel how long you've carried it. The bell holds the time.
Lavan. The four rounds of the Sikh wedding: four stanzas by Guru Ram Das, sung as the couple walks around the scripture. Today's word.
Your line: four rounds, one life. Today, keep one small promise to someone you love, on purpose, and notice it. Day fifty-six.

howItsDone: In the Anand Karaj, the Sikh wedding, the couple walks four times clockwise around the Guru Granth Sahib as each of Guru Ram Das's four lavan is read and then sung, joined by a scarf.
